evidence: Sly and Robbie came up in the same 1970s Kingston studio scene as King Tubby, working the same rhythm-as-raw-material logic dub established, though based mainly at Channel One rather than Tubby's own studio; no single documented session ties the two directly.

trackPair.whatToListenFor: Tubby empties a finished mix out until the rhythm is nearly all that's left. Sly and Robbie build the rhythm that way from the start: drum and bass carrying the song, everything else arranged around them rather than the other way around.

explanation.age7: King Tubby and the duo Sly and Robbie were both part of the same 1970s Kingston music scene, where the drums and bass became the most important part of a song.
explanation.age13: Sly and Robbie worked mostly at a different studio than Tubby, but they were shaped by the same idea that was taking over Kingston at the time: build the song around the rhythm, not around the singer.
explanation.adult: A scene-level claim rather than a documented collaboration: both acts are central to the same mid-1970s shift in Kingston studio practice toward rhythm-as-foundation, arrived at through overlapping but distinct studio lineages (Tubby's own desk versus the Channel One house band).
